newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Dutch Q4 cocoa grind offers no surprises - trade.
newsitem.headline: Dutch Q4 cocoa grind offers no surprises - trade.

text.p: Dutch cocoa traders said the fourth quarter grind figure released on Tuesday was roughly in line with expectations and unlikely to have any market impact.

The fourth quarter Dutch grind was up 3.90 percent to 97,273 tonnes against 93,619 tonnes in the same 1995 period. The figure brought the full-year 1996 total to 388,412 tonnes, up 9.26 percent from the 355,492 processed in 1995.
Industry sources had predicted a fourth quarter rise of around five percent.
"It was just below our forecast but near enough to make no difference. There were no surprises in the figure," one said.
The rise in the grind figure reflected continued good demand for cocoa powder and it would have been slightly greater but for one processor switching to process more cocoa liquor.
"Everyone knew the situation and that was incorporated into the forecasts," another trader said.
The growth trend in Dutch grinding is expected to continue through next year, with bulk shipments playing an increasinly large role for the major processors.
Louis Bensdorp, president of the Dutch Cocoa Association predicts some 400,000 tonnes of cocoa beans will be ground in the Netherlands in the current 1996/1997 season (Oct-Sept).

But the New Year has brought little change to a moribund physical market in Europe, beset by low participation from industry. Traders said sterling's strength was still hampering chocolate manufacturers' buying plans.
"You get the impression people would like to take some cover and they see the market coming down but the price in their local currencies is rising and it's very confusing," one said.
Traders said they were now looking for signs that arrivals from the Ivory Coast would begin to pick up this month to confirm forecasts of a reasonably large main crop.
